meta.title: OP-Bench research explorer
meta.scoreNote: Higher OP-Bench scores indicate less over-personalization.
meta.rqNote: The paper explicitly labels RQ1–RQ3. The RQ4 card presents the paper's supplementary timing analysis from Appendix Table 11.

categories.label: Irrelevance
categories.description: Unnecessary personal information enters an otherwise unrelated answer.

categories.label: Repetition
categories.description: Related queries receive near-identical personalized responses.

categories.label: Sycophancy
categories.description: The agent over-aligns with claims, memories, or values instead of staying accurate and balanced.

workflow.title: Turn long-horizon dialogue into a user model
workflow.description: LoCoMo multi-session conversations are converted into a structured representation of the user.
details: Treat speaker_a as the user and speaker_b as the assistant
Extract a concise profile, topics, and observations
Keep long-term facts separate from the current query

workflow.title: Create targeted over-personalization probes
workflow.description: Prompt templates turn the user model into neutral, baiting, sycophancy, and diversity-focused questions.
details: Irrelevance: fully irrelevant and deceptively relevant baiting
Sycophancy: fact, value, and fake-memory variants
Repetition: subtopics followed by open-ended questions

workflow.title: Filter for label accuracy and quality
workflow.description: Every constructed instance passes a two-reviewer quality-control loop before entering the benchmark.
details: Two independent annotators review every item
Disagreements are escalated to senior adjudication

rq1.title: Does over-personalization exist?
rq1.summary: Yes. Every evaluated memory-augmented method scores below its memory-free BASE counterpart on OP-Bench.
rq1.conclusion: Memory augmentation is consistently associated with over-personalization. More elaborate memory systems, including MemU and MEMOS, generally show larger degradation, while simple RAG is milder.

rq2.title: Why does over-personalization occur?
rq2.summary: The paper describes a memory-hijacking loop: memory is retrieved aggressively, receives disproportionate attention, and is applied indiscriminately.

evidence.label: Over-attention
evidence.title: Retrieved memory becomes a privileged signal
evidence.description: Length-normalized attention consistently favors retrieved memory tokens over the user's query across task settings.

evidence.label: Over-retrieval
evidence.title: Retrieval does not know when to abstain
evidence.description: Fully irrelevant questions still receive low-similarity memories, while baiting questions can retrieve highly similar memories that are nevertheless misleading.

evidence.label: Response collapse
evidence.title: Memory narrows the response space
evidence.description: Embedding distributions become more concentrated with memory, and language shifts toward agreement-oriented or deferential phrasing.

rq3.title: Can over-personalization be mitigated?
rq3.summary: Only partially. Post-processing can lift OP-Bench scores, but improvements often trade off against LoCoMo personalization performance and remain below the BASE oracle.

rq4.title: What is the timing cost of mitigation?
rq4.summary: The appendix latency breakdown shows that mitigation cost is dominated by post-processing and model response, not memory retrieval itself.
rq4.note: Timing is reported in Appendix Table 11; the main paper does not label this analysis as a separate RQ4.
